lead: A binomial count is the number of successes in a fixed number of independent yes/no trials, when every trial has the same success probability p. It exists because many real counts are made of repeated yes/no actions: payments that fail, cricket balls that hit a boundary, components that pass inspection. The binomial probability mass function gives the chance of exactly k successes in n trials. You will use it for quality checks, surveys, risk counts and A/B test results.
prereq: You need: random variables, expectation and variance from Unit 2; factorials; and binomial coefficients C(n,k).

sections.h3: Bernoulli trials and the binomial count

blocks.text: Call one trial Bernoulli when it has exactly two outcomes: success and failure. The success probability p is the same on every trial. Trials are independent: the result of one trial does not change p for the next.

Fix n before you start. Let X be the number of successes in those n trials. X can take only whole values 0,1,...,n. This X has a binomial distribution, written X ~ Bin(n,p). Some syllabi call it the Bernoulli counting distribution; the single-trial version is sometimes called the point binomial.

The probability of exactly k successes comes from two parts. First, choose which k of the n trials are successes; this can be done in C(n,k) ways. Second, every such pattern has probability pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. Multiply.

blocks.where: n is the fixed number of trials; p is the success probability on one trial; k is the number of successes; C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n−k)!) is the number of ways to choose k successes; 1 − p is the failure probability.

blocks.text: A single term P(X=k) is the probability mass function (pmf). The values add to 1 over k=0,...,n. In a phone exam, use a calculator or a binomial table for C(n,k); do not expand factorials by hand unless n is small.

sections.h3: Mean, variance and adding binomial counts

blocks.text: For X ~ Bin(n,p), the mean is E[X]=np. If you check 50 payments and each fails with p=0.1, the average number of failures is 50×0.1=5 payments. The variance is Var(X)=np(1−p). Its square root is the standard deviation. These formulas come from writing X as a sum of n independent 0/1 trial counts.
E[X] = np,   Var(X) = np(1 − p),   SD(X) = √(np(1 − p))
blocks.where: E[X] is the mean count; Var(X) is the variance; SD(X) is the standard deviation; n is the number of trials; p is the success probability.

blocks.text: The shape depends on p. At p = 0.5 the pmf is symmetric: P(X = k) = P(X = n − k). If p < 0.5 the pmf is skewed right, with a longer right tail. If p > 0.5 it is skewed left, with a longer left tail. For small n, read the pmf from the formula. For rare events with large n and small p, see Poisson distribution. For large n with np and n(1−p) both not small, the normal approximation is in normal distribution.

Independent binomial counts with the same p add. If X ~ Bin(n,p) and Y ~ Bin(m,p) are independent, then X+Y ~ Bin(n+m,p). The same p is required. Counts from groups with different p do not add to a binomial. This rule is used when two shifts or two servers combine counts under one failure rate.

You often need a range, not one exact value. P(X ≤ a) is the sum of the pmf from k=0 to k=a. For "at least a", use P(X ≥ a)=1−P(X ≤ a−1). For "between a and b" with whole-number limits, use P(X ≤ b)−P(X ≤ a−1). This avoids adding many terms one by one.

items: Write the range you need as whole-number limits for k.
For P(X ≤ a), add P(X=k) from k=0 to k=a.
For P(X ≥ a), compute 1 − P(X ≤ a−1).
For P(a ≤ X ≤ b), compute P(X ≤ b) − P(X ≤ a−1).

blocks.text: Check that every probability lies between 0 and 1. Check that the terms over all k add to 1; this catches a missing binomial coefficient. If n is large, direct sums are slow. The Poisson approximation helps when n is large and p is small; see Poisson distribution. The normal approximation helps when np and n(1−p) are both not small; see normal distribution. For exact exam answers, use the binomial formula or a binomial table unless the question asks for an approximation.

spec.title: Binomial count from ten trials
spec.aria: Four blocks show ten independent UPI trials, counting failures, and applying the binomial pmf with p = 0.2.

examples.question: A UPI payment fails with probability 0.2 independently. In 10 payments, find P(X = 3) and P(X ≤ 2).
steps: Define X = number of failed payments in n=10. X ~ Bin(10,0.2), so p=0.2 and q=1−p=0.8.
examples.answer: P(X = 3) = 0.2013 and P(X ≤ 2) = 0.6778; the chance of exactly three failures is 0.2013, and the chance of at most two failures is 0.6778.
examples.check:
import math
n = 10
p = 0.2
q = 1 - p
px3 = math.comb(n, 3) * p**3 * q**(n - 3)
pxle2 = sum(math.comb(n, k) * p**k * q**(n - k) for k in range(3))
print(round(px3, 4))
print(round(pxle2, 4))

traps: Using the binomial when p changes between trials. If each trial has a different success probability, the count is not Bin(n,p).
Forgetting the binomial coefficient C(n,k). The factor pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ alone is the probability of one particular pattern, not of all patterns with k successes.
"At most 2" means k=0,1,2, not k≤3. "At least 2" means k=2,...,n, often computed as 1−P(X≤1). "At least one" is 1−P(X=0).
Adding two binomial counts with different p. X+Y is binomial only when the success probability is the same and the groups are independent.
Confusing variance np(1−p) with standard deviation. The standard deviation is √(np(1−p)).

quiz.q: State the binomial pmf for X ~ Bin(n,p), with k = 0,1,...,n.
quiz.a: P(X = k) = C(n,k) pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, where C(n,k) is the number of ways to choose k successes from n trials.

quiz.q: Why do the trials need the same p and independence for a binomial count?
quiz.a: The same p keeps every pattern with k successes at probability pᵏ(1−p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. Independence keeps one trial from changing the next, so the product rule applies and the count has the binomial pmf. If p changes, the count is not Bin(n,p).

quiz.q: In 8 independent trials with success probability p = 0.25, find P(X = 2).
For X ~ Bin(10,0.2), find the mean, variance and standard deviation of X.
quiz.a: Mean = np = 10×0.2 = 2 failures. Variance = np(1−p) = 10×0.2×0.8 = 1.6 failures². SD = √1.6 ≈ 1.2649 failures.

quiz.q: For X ~ Bin(10,0.2), compare P(X=0) and P(X=1). What does the comparison say about the shape?
quiz.a: P(X=0)=0.8¹⁰=0.1074. P(X=1)=10×0.2×0.8⁹=0.2684. P(X=1) is larger than P(X=0). With p=0.2<0.5, the pmf has a longer right tail; the peak is near np=2, not at 0.

quiz.q: What does C(n,k) count in the binomial formula?
quiz.a: C(n,k)=n!/(k!(n−k)!) counts the number of ways to choose which k of the n trials are successes.

quiz.q: X ~ Bin(5,0.3) and Y ~ Bin(4,0.3) are independent. Give the distribution of X+Y.
quiz.a: Because both counts are independent and have the same success probability p=0.3, X+Y ~ Bin(5+4,0.3) = Bin(9,0.3).

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, binomial counts sit inside A/B testing, credit-card fraud alerts and server error budgets. The beta-binomial model adds uncertainty about p and is common in Bayesian work. Logistic regression uses a binomial likelihood for yes/no outcomes. Search next for beta-binomial distribution, binomial proportion confidence interval, and Poisson approximation to binomial.
